procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (implied, based on the existence of a Charge Sheet No.1 dated 07.05.2016)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Final judgment and order dated 10.09.2018 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Misc. Application No. 35 of 2017.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellants filed an application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 in the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (Criminal Misc. Application No. 35 of 2017) to quash Charge Sheet No.1 dated 07.05.2016. The Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court found that the High Court did not adequately examine the challenge to the proceedings or provide sufficient reasoning for its decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and remanded the case to the High Court with instructions to decide the application afresh on merits, after issuing notice to the respondents, and in accordance with law.

directions: The case is remanded to the High Court for its decision on merits uninfluenced by any of our observations in this order after notice to the respondents.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the appellants’ application filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 without providing a reasoned order.

facts: The appellants filed an application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) before the High Court to quash a charge sheet.
The Single Judge of the High Court dismissed this application.
The appellants appealed this dismissal to the Supreme Court.
law: A court deciding a case must first set out the brief facts to understand the controversy.
It must then examine the challenge made in light of established legal principles.
Finally, the court must record its findings and provide the reasons for its conclusion, explaining why a case for interference is or is not made out.
Providing a reasoned order is essential as it enables a higher court to examine whether the decision is factually and legally sustainable.
application: The Supreme Court examined the High Court's order and found that it only quoted legal principles laid down in previous decisions regarding the scope of Section 482 CrPC.

The High Court's order completely failed to mention the specific facts of the case, such as the nature of the complaint/FIR, the allegations against the appellants, or the grounds on which the proceedings were being challenged.
By not applying the legal principles to the specific facts, the High Court failed to perform the necessary judicial exercise of providing a reasoned analysis.
This omission left the Supreme Court unable to understand the factual basis of the case or to assess the correctness of the High Court's decision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in dismissing the application in such a manner. The disposal of the case without reference to its facts and without providing reasons was unsustainable. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and remanded the case for a fresh decision on the merits, to be made in accordance with the law and supported by reasons.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the appellants’ application filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 without providing a reasoned order.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's dismissal of the application was improper because the order lacked reasoning. A judicial order, especially one that disposes of a case, must set out the facts, examine the legal challenges, and provide reasons for its conclusion to allow for scrutiny by a higher court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A judicial order must set out the factual matrix of the case, examine the legal challenges in light of established principles, and record reasoned findings to support its conclusion. This is the minimum requirement to enable a higher court to determine if the reasoning is factually and legally sustainable.
obiter: Having formed an opinion to remand the case in the light of our reasoning, we do not consider it proper to go into the merits of the case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's order was unsustainable because it only quoted general principles of law regarding Section 482 Cr.P.C. but failed to set out the specific facts of the case, appreciate the factual controversy, examine the legal challenges in light of those facts, and record any findings or reasons for its conclusion. The court failed to mention the nature of the complaint/FIR, the allegations, who filed it, the grounds of challenge, or why those grounds were not made out.
legal_tests_applied: A court disposing of a case must first set out the brief facts to understand the factual matrix, then examine the challenge made to the proceedings in light of the principles of law, and then record its finding as to on what basis and for what reasons a case is made out for interference or not.
policy_considerations: Providing reasons in a judicial order is the minimum requirement to support a conclusion, as it enables a higher court to examine whether the reasoning given by the lower court is factually and legally sustainable.
